claims.text: Polycrystalline copper has a face-centered cubic crystal structure at ambient temperature and pressure.
Polycrystalline FCC copper exhibits high ductility under ambient quasi-static loading.
The high ductility of copper is attributable to multiple {111} slip systems in its FCC structure.
Copper has a low stacking-fault energy that facilitates efficient dislocation nucleation and glide.
Molecular dynamics simulations can systematically vary stacking-fault energy and grain-boundary structure in model polycrystalline copper.
The relevant structural mediator consists of abundant {111} slip planes and typical grain-boundary configurations in FCC copper.
Low stacking-fault energy enables dislocation nucleation and propagation along multiple {111} slip systems.
Dislocation propagation along multiple slip systems permits plastic deformation without premature fracture.
Favorable stacking-fault characteristics in copper will increase ductile strain and sustain plastic deformation.
Favorable stacking-fault characteristics will produce a higher density of dislocations propagating on {111} planes than modifications that impede these processes.
Standard polycrystalline copper with its inherent stacking-fault energy and grain structure is the appropriate baseline.
The proposed mechanism is applicable to conventional FCC metals under ambient quasi-static loading.
The proposed mechanism may not extend to non-FCC materials, extreme temperatures, or very high strain rates.
The quantitative sensitivity of copper ductility to stacking-fault energy and grain-boundary structure is not defined.
Ductile strain before failure, dislocation activity on {111} systems, and stress-strain curves can be measured to test the hypothesis.

Failure to obtain consistent and reproducible changes in dislocation behavior and ductile strain after modifying stacking-fault energy and grain-boundary character would falsify the proposed causal account.
